## Goals for this section

-   Add many predictors
-   Be able to interpret and visualize MR
-   Know how to do factorial ANOVA models
-   Be able to model, interpret, and visualize interactions

## Moving to many predictors

```{r}
#| code-fold: true
library(brms)
library(modelr)
library(patchwork)
library(tidyverse)
library(tidybayes)

# normal density
p1 <-
  tibble(x = seq(from = -3, to = 3, by = .1)) %>% 
  ggplot(aes(x = x, ymin = 0, ymax = (dnorm(x)) / max(dnorm(x)))) +
  geom_ribbon(fill = "steelblue4", color = "steelblue4", alpha = .6) +
  annotate(geom = "text",
           x = 0, y = .2,
           label = "normal",
           size = 7) +
  annotate(geom = "text",
           x = c(0, 1.5), y = .6,
           label = c("italic(M)[0]", "italic(S)[0]"), 
           size = 7, family = "Times", parse = T) +
  scale_x_continuous(expand = c(0, 0)) +
  theme_void() +
  theme(axis.line.x = element_line(linewidth = 0.5))

# a second normal density
p2 <-
  tibble(x = seq(from = -3, to = 3, by = .1)) %>% 
  ggplot(aes(x = x, ymin = 0, ymax = (dnorm(x)) / max(dnorm(x)))) +
  geom_ribbon(fill = "steelblue4", color = "steelblue4", alpha = .6) +
  annotate(geom = "text",
           x = 0, y = .2,
           label = "normal",
           size = 7) +
  annotate(geom = "text",
           x = c(0, 1.5), y = .6,
           label = c("italic(M)[italic(j)]", "italic(S)[italic(j)]"), 
           size = 7, family = "Times", parse = T) +
  scale_x_continuous(expand = c(0, 0)) +
  theme_void() +
  theme(axis.line.x = element_line(linewidth = 0.5))

## two annotated arrows
# save our custom arrow settings
my_arrow <- arrow(angle = 20, length = unit(0.35, "cm"), type = "closed")
p3 <-
  tibble(x    = c(.33, 1.67),
         y    = c(1, 1),
         xend = c(.67, 1.2),
         yend = c(0, 0)) %>%
  
  ggplot(aes(x = x, xend = xend,

  x = c(.35, 1.3), y = .5,
  label = "'~'",

# exponential density

  tibble(x = seq(from = 0, to = 1, by = .01)) %>% 
  ggplot(aes(x = x, ymin = 0, ymax = (dexp(x, 2) / max(dexp(x, 2))))) +

           x = .5, y = .2,

  annotate(geom = "text",

           label = "italic(K)",

  scale_x_continuous(expand = c(0, 0)) +
  theme_void() +
  theme(axis.line.x = element_line(linewidth = 0.5))

# likelihood formula
p5 <-
  tibble(x = .5,
         y = .25,
         label = "beta[0]+sum()[italic(j)]*beta[italic(j)]*italic(x)[italic(ji)]") %>% 
  
  ggplot(aes(x = x, y = y, label = label)) +
  geom_text(size = 7, parse = T, family = "Times") +
  scale_x_continuous(expand = c(0, 0), limits = c(0, 1)) +
  ylim(0, 1) +
  theme_void()
  
  # half-normal density
p6 <-
  tibble(x = seq(from = 0, to = 3, by = .01)) %>% 
  ggplot(aes(x = x, ymin = 0, ymax = (dnorm(x)) / max(dnorm(x)))) +

# three annotated arrows

  tibble(x    = c( .43, 1.5, 2.5),

# student-t density
p8 <-
  tibble(x = seq(from = -3, to = 3, by = .1)) %>% 
  ggplot(aes(x = x, ymin = 0, ymax = (dt(x, 3) / max(dt(x, 3))))) +
  geom_ribbon(fill = "steelblue4", color = "steelblue4", alpha = .6) +

# the final annotated arrow
p9 <-
  tibble(x     = c(.375, .625),
         y     = c(1/3, 1/3),
         label = c("'~'", "italic(i)")) %>%

  ggplot(aes(x = x, y = y, label = label)) +
  geom_text(size = c(10, 7), parse = T, family = "Times") +
  geom_segment(x = .5, xend = .5,
               y = 1, yend = 0,
               arrow = my_arrow) +

# some text
p10 <-
  tibble(x     = .5,
         y     = .5,
         label = "italic(y[i])") %>% 
  
  ggplot(aes(x = x, y = y, label = label)) +
  geom_text(size = 7, parse = T, family = "Times") +
  xlim(0, 1) +
  theme_void()

# define the layout
layout <- c(
  area(t = 1, b = 2, l = 3, r = 5),
  area(t = 1, b = 2, l = 7, r = 9),
  area(t = 4, b = 5, l = 1, r = 3),
  area(t = 4, b = 5, l = 5, r = 7),
  area(t = 4, b = 5, l = 9, r = 11),
  area(t = 3, b = 4, l = 3, r = 9),
  area(t = 7, b = 8, l = 5, r = 7),
  area(t = 6, b = 7, l = 1, r = 11),
  area(t = 9, b = 9, l = 5, r = 7),
  area(t = 10, b = 10, l = 5, r = 7)
)

# combine and plot!
(p1 + p2 + p4 + p5 + p6 + p3 + p8 + p7 + p9 + p10) + 
  plot_layout(design = layout) &
  ylim(0, 1) &
  theme(plot.margin = margin(0, 5.5, 0, 5.5))
```

## Your turn: write the equation

Can you write this model equation? Assume two IVs.

## data

```{r}
#| code-fold: true
#| 
MR <- read.csv("hw3.csv")   # also at https://bayes27.netlify.app/hw3.csv
MR <- MR %>% 
  mutate(SS_c = `schoool.success` - mean(`schoool.success`),
         FQ_c = `friendship.quality` - mean(`friendship.quality`),
         iv = `intervention.group`) %>% 
        mutate(iv = as.factor(iv))

MR <- MR %>%
  mutate(iv.d = case_match(iv, "1" ~ "control", "2" ~ "tx", "3" ~ "tx"))

MR
```

## Describing the data

```{r}
#| code-fold: true
library(psych)
describe(MR)
```

## model

happiness \~ Normal( $\mu_i$ , $\sigma$ )

$\mu_i$ = $\beta_0$ + $\beta_1$ $SS\_c$ + $\beta_2$ $FQ\_c$

$\beta_0$ \~ Normal(5, 2)\
$\beta_1$ \~ Normal(0, 2)\
$\beta_2$ \~ Normal(0, 2)\
$\sigma$ \~ Exponential(1)

## Fitting the model

```{r}
mr.1 <- 
  brm(family = gaussian,
      happiness ~ 1 + SS_c + FQ_c,
      prior = c(prior(normal(5, 2), class = Intercept),
                prior(normal(0, 2), class = b, coef = SS_c),
                prior(normal(0, 2), class = b, coef = FQ_c),
                prior(exponential(1), class = sigma)),
      iter = 2000, warmup = 1000, chains = 2, cores = 2,
      data = MR,
      backend = "cmdstanr",
      sample_prior = "yes",
      file = "mr.1")
```

## Equivalent notation

equivalent notation

```{r, eval=FALSE}

library(brms)
mr.1 <- 
  brm(family = gaussian,
      happiness ~ 1 + SS_c + FQ_c,

                prior(normal(0, 2), class = b),
                prior(exponential(1), class = sigma)),
      iter = 2000, warmup = 1000, chains = 2, cores = 2,
      data = MR,
      sample_prior = "yes",
```


## Prior predictive checks

```{r}
#| code-fold: true
prior.mr1 %>% 
  slice_sample(n = 100) %>% 
  rownames_to_column("draw") %>% 
  expand(nesting(draw, Intercept, b_SS_c),
         a = c(-10, 10)) %>% 
  mutate(d = Intercept + b_SS_c * a) %>% 
  
  ggplot(aes(x = a, y = d)) +
  geom_line(aes(group = draw), alpha = .4) +
  labs(x = "Centered School Success",
       y = "happiness") +
  coord_cartesian(ylim = c(0, 10)) +
  theme_bw() +
  theme(panel.grid = element_blank()) 
```

```{r}
                prior(exponential(.5), class = sigma)),
```

## Conditional plots

-   Remember, anytime we have a multiple regression we are working with a 3d (or higher) response plane (in frequentist land), and in Bayesian we are working with a hyperdimensional mountain.

-   Regardless of what estimation we are using, we need to communicate our effects in simple terms, usually by restricting to only one variable at a time.

-   To do so, we need to either average across or pick a point on the other variables in the model to visualize our effect of interest


```{r}
spread_draws(b_Intercept, b_SS_c, b_FQ_c, sigma))
```

## Two+ categorical variables

```{r}
#| code-fold: true
MR <- MR %>% 
  mutate(iv = factor(iv),
         happy_c = happiness - mean(happiness),
         # a second factor: SES split at the median (just to have a 2nd categorical
         # variable to work with; in practice keep SES continuous, as we do later)
         iv2 = factor(if_else(SES > median(SES), "high SES", "low SES"),
                      levels = c("low SES", "high SES")))

MR %>% count(iv, iv2)
```

## Two factors: one index, one dummy

```{r}
#| code-fold: true
mr.5 <- 
  brm(family = gaussian,
      happiness ~ 0 + iv + iv2,
      prior = c(prior(normal(5, 2), class = b),
                prior(exponential(1), class = sigma)),
      iter = 2000, warmup = 1000, chains = 2, cores = 2,
      data = MR,
      backend = "cmdstanr",
      file = "mr.5b")
```

## brms non-linear syntax

{brms} does not automatically create index variables for more than 1 categorical variable. The `0 +` treats the first variable as an index but not the second, such that the second has a standard dummy interpretation.

We need a new syntax to write the model we want. We will use non-linear syntax for this, and revisit the syntax later in the class for additional models.

For ANOVA I've found centering or standardizing your DV is helpful

## Non-linear syntax: two index variables

```{r}
#| code-fold: true
mr.6 <- 
  brm(family = gaussian,
      bf(happy_c ~  a + b, # define 2 predictors
         a ~ 0 + iv, # specify the predictors
         b ~ 0 + iv2,
         nl = TRUE), # use non-linear syntax
      prior = c(prior(normal(0, 2), nlpar = a),
                prior(normal(0, 2), nlpar = b),
                prior(exponential(1), class = sigma)),
      iter = 2000, warmup = 1000, chains = 4, cores = 4,
      data = MR,
      backend = "cmdstanr",
      file = "mr.6b")


```

## Non-linear results

```{r}
summary(mr.6)
```

## Group means (centered DV)

```{r}
get_variables(mr.6)
```

```{r}
#| code-fold: true
mr.6 %>%
  gather_draws(b_a_iv1, b_a_iv2, b_a_iv3) %>%
  ggplot(aes(y = .variable, x = .value)) +
  stat_dotsinterval()

```

## Add the mean of the DV back in

Add the mean of your DV back in

```{r}
#| code-fold: true
mean_happy <- mean(MR$happiness)   # 5.21: we centered the DV, so add it back
mr.6 %>%
  spread_draws(b_a_iv1, b_a_iv2, b_a_iv3) %>%
  mutate(iv1 = b_a_iv1 + mean_happy) %>% 
  mutate(iv2 = b_a_iv2 + mean_happy) %>% 
  mutate(iv3 = b_a_iv3 + mean_happy) %>% 
  gather_draws(iv1, iv2, iv3) %>% 
  ggplot(aes(y = .variable, x = .value)) +
  stat_dotsinterval()

```

## Group means, summarized

```{r}
#| code-fold: true
mr.6 %>%
  spread_draws(b_a_iv1, b_a_iv2, b_a_iv3) %>%
  mutate(iv1 = b_a_iv1 + mean_happy) %>% 
  mutate(iv2 = b_a_iv2 + mean_happy) %>% 
  mutate(iv3 = b_a_iv3 + mean_happy) %>% 
  gather_draws(iv1, iv2, iv3) %>% 
  mean_qi()
```

```{r}
#| code-fold: true
MR %>%
  group_by(iv) %>%
  summarise(mean = mean(happiness), n = n())
```

## Each draw is a population

Each posterior row suggests a different population we are drawing from, much like each row represents a different regression line

```{r}
#| code-fold: true
MR %>%
  data_grid(iv, .model = MR) %>%
  add_epred_draws(mr.6, dpar = c("mu", "sigma")) %>%
  sample_draws(50) %>%
  mutate(mu = mu + mean_happy) %>% 
  ggplot(aes(y = iv)) +
  stat_dist_slab(aes(dist = "norm", arg1 = mu, arg2 = sigma),
    slab_color = "gray65", alpha = 1/10, fill = NA) +
  geom_point(aes(x = happiness), data = MR, shape = 21, fill = "#9ECAE1", size = 2)
```

## comparing levels ie contrasts

We could do this "by hand" or with compare_levels

```{r}
mr.6 %>%
  gather_draws(b_a_iv1, b_a_iv2, b_a_iv3) %>%
  compare_levels(.value, by = .variable) %>%
  ggplot(aes(y = .variable, x = .value)) +
  stat_halfeye()
```

## The draws, long format

```{r}
mr.6 %>%
  gather_draws(b_a_iv1, b_a_iv2, b_a_iv3) 
```

## compare_levels() output

```{r}
mr.6 %>%
  gather_draws(b_a_iv1, b_a_iv2, b_a_iv3) %>%
  compare_levels(.value, by = .variable) 
```

## Summarizing the contrasts

```{r}
mr.6 %>%
  gather_draws(b_a_iv1, b_a_iv2, b_a_iv3) %>%
  compare_levels(.value, by = .variable) %>%
  group_by(.variable) %>%  
  mode_qi(.value)
```

## An index for every cell

What about an *interaction* between two categorical variables? The simplest index-coded version gives every **cell** (every combination of `iv` and `iv2`) its own mean, with one prior for all six:

```{r}
#| code-fold: true
mr.7 <- 
  brm(family = gaussian,
      happy_c ~ 0 + iv:iv2,
      prior = c(prior(normal(0, 2), class = b),
                prior(exponential(1), class = sigma)),
      iter = 2000, warmup = 1000, chains = 4, cores = 4,
      data = MR,
      backend = "cmdstanr",
      file = "mr.7")
fixef(mr.7)
```

## Is there an interaction? Ask the cell means {.smaller}

With cell means, "is there an interaction?" becomes "does the high − low SES difference change across `iv`?", a difference of differences computed from the draws:

```{r}
#| code-fold: true
#| fig-height: 3.5
cells <- avg_predictions(mr.7, by = c("iv", "iv2")) %>% get_draws()

cells %>% 
  mutate(draw = draw + mean_happy) %>% 
  ggplot(aes(x = iv, y = draw, color = iv2, group = iv2)) +
  stat_pointinterval(position = position_dodge(width = .3)) +
  stat_summary(fun = median, geom = "line", position = position_dodge(width = .3)) +
  labs(y = "happiness", color = NULL)
```

## Difference of differences

The high − low SES gap in each `iv` group, then how much those gaps differ between groups (that's the interaction):

```{r}
#| code-fold: true
cells %>% 
  select(drawid, iv, iv2, draw) %>% 
  pivot_wider(names_from = iv2, values_from = draw) %>% 
  mutate(ses_diff = `high SES` - `low SES`) %>% 
  select(drawid, iv, ses_diff) %>% 
  pivot_wider(names_from = iv, values_from = ses_diff, names_prefix = "iv") %>% 
  transmute(`iv2 vs iv1` = iv2 - iv1, `iv3 vs iv1` = iv3 - iv1, `iv3 vs iv2` = iv3 - iv2) %>% 
  pivot_longer(everything()) %>% 
  group_by(name) %>% 
  median_qi(value)
```


## A 3×2 factorial: the data

```{r}
anova <- read_csv("anova.csv")   # also at https://bayes27.netlify.app/anova.csv
anova <- anova %>% 
  mutate(SupportLevel = cut(Support, breaks = c(0, 5, 10, 18), labels = c("low", "med", "high")),
         condition = factor(group))   # renamed: marginaleffects reserves the name "group"
anova %>% count(condition, SupportLevel)
```

If we want to fit a 3×2 ANOVA, what linear model are we running?

## The 3×2 model, in brms's names {.smaller}

$$\text{Anxiety}_i \sim \text{Normal}(\mu_i, \sigma)$$

$$
\begin{aligned}
\mu_i = \beta_0 &+ \beta_1\,\text{conditionTx}_i + \beta_2\,\text{SupportLevelmed}_i + \beta_3\,\text{SupportLevelhigh}_i \\
&+ \beta_4\,(\text{conditionTx} \times \text{SupportLevelmed})_i + \beta_5\,(\text{conditionTx} \times \text{SupportLevelhigh})_i
\end{aligned}
$$

Each name is a 0/1 dummy, exactly as it will appear in `summary()`. The reference cell (all dummies = 0) is Control with low support, so $\beta_0$ is that cell's mean and every other coefficient is a difference from it.

## Fitting the factorial model

```{r}
#| code-fold: true
mr.8b <- 
  brm(family = gaussian,
      Anxiety ~ condition * SupportLevel,
      prior = c(prior(normal(5, 3), class = Intercept),
                prior(normal(0, 2), class = b, coef = conditionTx),
                prior(normal(0, 2), class = b, coef = SupportLevelhigh),
                prior(normal(0, 2), class = b, coef = SupportLevelmed),
                prior(normal(0, 2), class = b, coef = conditionTx:SupportLevelhigh),
                prior(normal(0, 2), class = b, coef = conditionTx:SupportLevelmed),
                prior(student_t(3, 0, 2.5), class = sigma)),
      iter = 2000, warmup = 1000, chains = 2, cores = 2,
      data = anova,
      sample_prior = "yes",
      backend = "cmdstanr",
      file = "mr.8b")
```

## Factorial results

```{r}
summary(mr.8b)
```

## Parameter names

```{r}
#| code-fold: true
get_variables(mr.8b)
```

## Cell means by hand: the dummy codes

How could we get posterior means for each of the 6 cells? Feed the 0/1 codes into the equation, draw by draw.

```{r}
contrasts(anova$condition)
```

```{r}
contrasts(anova$SupportLevel)
```

## Cell means by hand

```{r}
#| code-fold: true
mr.8b %>% 
  spread_draws(b_Intercept, b_conditionTx, b_SupportLevelmed, b_SupportLevelhigh,
               `b_conditionTx:SupportLevelmed`, `b_conditionTx:SupportLevelhigh`) %>% 
  mutate(Con_Lo  = b_Intercept,
         Con_Med = b_Intercept + b_SupportLevelmed,
         Con_Hi  = b_Intercept + b_SupportLevelhigh,
         Tx_Lo   = b_Intercept + b_conditionTx,
         Tx_Med  = b_Intercept + b_conditionTx + b_SupportLevelmed + `b_conditionTx:SupportLevelmed`,
         Tx_Hi   = b_Intercept + b_conditionTx + b_SupportLevelhigh + `b_conditionTx:SupportLevelhigh`) %>% 
  select(.draw, Con_Lo:Tx_Hi)
```

## A difference of cell means, by hand

```{r}
#| code-fold: true
mr.8b %>% 
  spread_draws(b_Intercept, b_SupportLevelmed, b_SupportLevelhigh) %>% 
  mutate(Con_Med = b_Intercept + b_SupportLevelmed,
         Con_Hi  = b_Intercept + b_SupportLevelhigh,
         hi_med_diff = Con_Hi - Con_Med) %>% 
  mean_qi(hi_med_diff)
```

## Getting cell means: options

1.  Compute them by hand from the draws (what we just did)
2.  Feed the same arithmetic to brms's `hypothesis()` (handy with LOTS of parameters, as in MLMs)
3.  Let a package do it: {marginaleffects} (what we'll use), or {emmeans}, which also works with brms models

## marginaleffects: what it does by default {.smaller}

From here on, {marginaleffects} is our main tool for contrasts and slopes. It makes choices for you; know them:

-   **The grid.** With no `newdata`, it makes a prediction for *every row of your data*. `avg_*()` then **averages** those, e.g. averaging over the observed mix of groups. Not the same as a "typical" person (`newdata = "mean"`) or all factor combinations equally (`newdata = "balanced"`); next slides show two grids, two answers.
-   **The summary.** For a brms model, `estimate` is the posterior **median**, and the interval is equal-tailed (quantile) at 95%.
-   **The scale.** `type = "response"` (the default) vs. `"link"`. It doesn't matter yet, but it will for logistic and count models.
-   **The escape hatch.** `get_draws()` turns any result back into one row per draw, so you can check it by hand or plot it with tidybayes.

## Support-level means, averaged over the observed data

```{r}
avg_predictions(mr.8b, by = "SupportLevel")
```

## ...or over a balanced grid

Each support level averaged over Control and Tx *equally*, regardless of how many people were in each cell:

```{r}
avg_predictions(mr.8b, newdata = "balanced", by = "SupportLevel")
```

## All six cell means

```{r}
predictions(mr.8b, newdata = datagrid(SupportLevel = unique, condition = unique))
```

## Pairwise contrasts between support levels

```{r}
avg_predictions(mr.8b, by = "SupportLevel", hypothesis = "pairwise")
# newer marginaleffects versions write this as  hypothesis = ~ pairwise
```

## Tx vs. Control within each support level

```{r}
comparisons(mr.8b, variables = "condition", by = "SupportLevel")
```

If the Tx − Control difference changes across support levels, that's the interaction.

## Plotting the contrasts

```{r}
#| code-fold: true
#| fig-height: 3.5
avg_predictions(mr.8b, by = "SupportLevel", hypothesis = "pairwise") %>% 
  get_draws() %>% 
  ggplot(aes(x = draw, y = term)) +
  stat_halfeye() +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, linetype = 2) +
  labs(x = "difference in anxiety", y = NULL)
```

## The interaction, plotted

```{r}
#| code-fold: true
#| fig-height: 4
avg_predictions(mr.8b, by = c("SupportLevel", "condition")) %>% 
  get_draws() %>% 
  ggplot(aes(x = SupportLevel, y = draw, color = condition)) +
  geom_jitter(data = anova, aes(y = Anxiety), alpha = .4, width = .15) +
  stat_pointinterval(position = position_dodge(width = .4)) +
  facet_grid(~ condition) +
  labs(y = "Anxiety", color = NULL) +
  theme(legend.position = "none")
```

## Interactions

Continuing our translation of previous skills to a Bayesian framework.

Interactions reflect when the influence of one variable depends on another. No longer can speak of main effects, now one needs to describe the association between two (or more) variables and the DV. The result is that the interpretation is the hard part, not necessarily the modeling.

As models get more complex, interactions become more likely (anytime there is a boundary in the DV)

## Nominal plus metric/continuous interaction

```{r}
#| code-fold: true
mr.12 <-
  brm(family = gaussian,
      happiness ~ 0 + iv.d + SS_c,
      prior = c(prior(normal(5, 3), class = b, coef = iv.dcontrol),
                prior(normal(5, 3), class = b, coef = iv.dtx),
                prior(normal(0, .5), class = b, coef = SS_c),
                prior(exponential(1), class = sigma)),
      iter = 2000, warmup = 1000, chains = 4, cores = 4,
      data = MR, 
      backend = "cmdstanr",
      file = "mr.12")
```

## Results: parallel slopes

```{r}
summary(mr.12)
```

## Parallel lines by group

```{r}
#| code-fold: true
MR %>%
  group_by(iv.d) %>%
  data_grid(SS_c = seq_range(SS_c, n = 50), .model = MR) %>%
  add_epred_draws(mr.12, ndraws = 100) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = SS_c, y = happiness, color = iv.d)) +
  geom_line(aes(y = .epred, group = paste(iv.d, .draw)),alpha = .1) +
  geom_point(data = MR) 
```

```{r}
mr.14 %>%
  spread_draws(`b_SS_c`, `b_iv.dtx:SS_c`) %>%

  mutate(slope.tx = `b_SS_c` + `b_iv.dtx:SS_c`) %>%
```

## Three groups × a continuous predictor

The same idea with all three intervention groups and a continuous moderator (SES). With three groups, the "effect of SES" is three slopes, and the interaction asks whether they differ. This is where marginaleffects saves a lot of hand computation.

```{r}
a.4 <- 
  brm(family = gaussian,
      happiness ~ 1 + iv*SES,
      prior = c(prior(normal(5, 5), class = b),
                prior(exponential(1), class = sigma)),
      iter = 2000, warmup = 1000, chains = 2, cores = 2,
      data = MR,
      sample_prior = "yes",
      backend = "cmdstanr",
      file = "a.4")

```

## 3-group × SES results

```{r}
summary(a.4)
```

```{r}
plot_predictions(a.4, condition = "iv")
```

## Continuous interaction example

```{r}
#| code-fold: true
Multipleregression <- read.csv("Multipleregression.csv")



Multipleregression$Support.r <- (17.36 - Multipleregression$Support)/3

mr.model <- lm(Stress ~ Support.r + Anxiety, data = Multipleregression)
library(visreg)
visreg2d(mr.model,"Support.r", "Anxiety", plot.type = "persp")

```

## Adding the interaction

```{r}
#| code-fold: true
Multipleregression  <- read_csv("Multipleregression.csv")

Multipleregression$Support.r <- (17.36 - Multipleregression$Support)/3

mr.model <- lm(Stress ~ Support.r* Anxiety, data = Multipleregression)
library(visreg)
visreg2d(mr.model,"Support.r", "Anxiety", plot.type = "persp")

```

## Default priors for the interaction model

```{r}
get_prior(family = gaussian,
      happiness ~ 1 + SS_c * FQ_c,data = MR)
```

## Fitting the interaction model

```{r}
mr.15 <- 
  brm(family = gaussian,
      happiness ~ 1 + SS_c * FQ_c,
      prior = c(prior(normal(0, 3), class = Intercept),
                prior(normal(0, 2), class = b, coef = SS_c),
                prior(normal(0, 2), class = b, coef = FQ_c),
                prior(normal(0, 2), class = b, coef = SS_c:FQ_c),
                prior(exponential(1), class = sigma)),
      iter = 2000, warmup = 1000, chains = 2, cores = 2,
      data = MR,
      sample_prior = "yes",
       backend = "cmdstanr",
      file = "mr.15")
```

## Interaction results

```{r}
summary(mr.15)
```
